headline: Parliament Advances RMA Overhaul and Climate-Liability Bill Amid Disputes Over Rights and Business
summary: Parliament advanced two major resource-management bills and a bill restricting climate-related tort claims, with coalition MPs arguing the changes would support growth and give businesses certainty while opponents warned of weaker environmental protections and reduced access to the courts. Question time was dominated by criticism of the Prime Minister’s remarks about businesses and his handling of Foreign Minister Winston Peters’ comments about China. MPs also debated a Northland expressway project, teacher-training expansion and the transfer of land to the Te Here ā Nuku Trust.

topicSummaries.topic: Luxon Faces Questions Over Remarks About Small Businesses
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The exchange put the Government’s relationship with small businesses under scrutiny as owners face difficult economic conditions.
topicSummaries.content: Labour leader Chris Hipkins repeatedly questioned Prime Minister Christopher Luxon about remarks linking businesses with a “parent-child mentality” and relying on the Government. Luxon said he had apologised for how his comments came across, while arguing that his broader point was about governments enabling businesses rather than directing them. Finance Minister Nicola Willis said the comments were not specifically directed at small businesses; Labour MPs argued the remarks risked dismissing the pressures business owners face. Small Business Minister Cameron Brewer defended the Government’s focus on creating conditions for growth.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Does he stand by his view that small-business owners who are struggling through tough economic conditions have created a parent-child mentality?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Well, look, I addressed those comments extensively and publicly yesterday, apologising for how they came across, and I could have expressed myself better.

topicSummaries.topic: Resource-Management Bills Pass Second Reading Amid Environmental and Treaty Disputes
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed replacement for the Resource Management Act will shape how homes, infrastructure and businesses are approved, as well as how environmental protections and Māori participation are handled.
topicSummaries.content: The Natural Environment Bill and Planning Bill both passed their second readings with support from National, ACT and New Zealand First, and opposition from Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori. The Government said the two-bill system would simplify planning, reduce consenting delays and enable development while retaining environmental limits. Changes include a wider route for some activities to proceed despite breaching limits where there is a net public benefit, removal of the precautionary principle and a longer transition period. Labour and Green MPs argued that the bills weaken environmental safeguards, create uncertainty and give Ministers too much discretion; Te Pāti Māori speakers objected to changes to Treaty-related arrangements and the removal of Mana Whakahono ā Rohe agreements. The bills now proceed to committee-of-the-whole-House consideration.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Bishop (National)
keyExchanges.quote: These reforms will make it easier to build homes, deliver infrastructure, and invest in productive businesses by reducing unnecessary cost, complexity, and delay.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rachel Brooking (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: These bills are not about efficiency; they will do the opposite of efficiency, and that is that they are going to create great inefficiencies, and we will not move forward with our plans in this country for many, many years.

topicSummaries.topic: Climate-Liability Bill Advances, Blocking Climate-Related Tort Claims
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill would prevent people from pursuing climate-related tort claims against greenhouse-gas emitters, including a case already before the courts.
topicSummaries.content: The Climate Change Response (Tort Liability) Amendment Bill passed its second reading with coalition support. The Government said the measure would prevent a court-created regime from operating alongside Parliament’s climate framework and reduce uncertainty for businesses. Labour, Green and Te Pāti Māori speakers argued that it would shut down Mike Smith’s case against Fonterra and other emitters before the substantive hearing, as well as bar future climate-related tort claims. They raised concerns about access to justice, the separation of powers and the bill’s development; the Government maintained that climate policy should be set through legislation and the executive. The bill has not yet completed its remaining stages.

keyExchanges.speaker: James Meager (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The purpose of this bill is to avoid that risk of having two parallel schemes.

keyExchanges.speaker: Camilla Belich (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: This bill does something quite significant: it shuts the door on a case that is already before the courts, and it shuts the door on any future tort claims relating to climate change emissions.

topicSummaries.topic: Luxon Defends Confidence in Peters After China Remarks
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The dispute raised questions about the standards expected of senior ministers and the Government’s response to remarks affecting Chinese New Zealanders and relations with a major trading partner.
topicSummaries.content: Hipkins and Green co-leader Marama Davidson pressed Luxon over Foreign Minister Winston Peters’ comments about Chinese people and China’s ambassador, which Luxon had previously described as racist and offensive. Luxon said Peters made the remarks as New Zealand First leader during a general debate, while saying he had raised his objections with the minister and remained confident in the New Zealand–China relationship. He also pointed to the approaching election. Davidson’s request for an urgent debate about China’s formal complaint was declined by the Speaker, who said the Government was not responsible for another government’s actions; a separate request concerning Luxon’s response was ruled out of time.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: How can he have confidence in a Minister of Foreign Affairs who makes comments that he himself has called racist?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Well, because he made the comments in a general debate speaking as the New Zealand First Leader, not while exercising his Foreign Affairs functions.

topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed road is intended to improve the Auckland–Northland connection, reduce travel disruption and change traffic through Wellsford and Te Hana.
topicSummaries.content: Transport Minister Chris Bishop said the Crown had finalised an agreement with the Northway consortium to design, build, finance, maintain and operate the first section of the Northern Expressway, from Warkworth to Te Hana. The Government put the project’s net present value at $3.649 billion and said the public-private partnership was about $250 million cheaper than traditional procurement. The 26-kilometre, four-lane route is expected to include interchanges, bridges and twin tunnels. Bishop cited forecast reductions in serious crashes, travel times and weather-related closures; those are projected benefits, not outcomes already achieved.

keyExchanges.speaker: Grant McCallum (National)
keyExchanges.quote: What does the first stage of the Northland Expressway include and what are its benefits?

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Bishop (National)
keyExchanges.quote: It’s a new 26-kilometre, four-lane expressway, with grade separated interchanges at Warkworth, Wellsford, and Te Hana.

topicSummaries.topic: Crimes Amendment Bill Reaches Third-Reading Debate
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill would change criminal offences and enforcement powers affecting retailers, first responders, corrections staff and people prosecuted for theft or violence.
topicSummaries.content: The House began debating the Crimes Amendment Bill at its final reading, but the debate was interrupted and adjourned, so the bill did not pass its third reading that day. Justice Minister James Meager said the bill would create or strengthen offences relating to strikes to the head or neck, assaults on first responders and frontline corrections staff, retail theft, and human trafficking and slavery. Labour and Green MPs supported the trafficking provisions but opposed other measures, questioning the scope of citizen’s-arrest powers and the effects of increased penalties for some theft offences. Labour MP Camilla Belich cited Ministry of Justice estimates of a substantial rise in the number of women in prison from the theft-penalty changes.

keyExchanges.speaker: James Meager (National)
keyExchanges.quote: This bill also responds to calls for a tougher approach to crime by creating new offences, strengthening existing penalties, and providing law enforcement with more tools to respond to criminal conduct.

keyExchanges.speaker: Camilla Belich (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The rest of this bill, although intended to decrease the victims of crime, may in some instances actually increase victimisations in New Zealand.

topicSummaries.topic: Nelson Tenths Land-Transfer Bill Passes Second Reading
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The legislation provides for land to be legally transferred to the trust representing descendants of customary owners after a long-running dispute over promised reserves.
topicSummaries.content: The Te Here ā Nuku (Nelson Tenths) Bill passed its second reading, with speakers from across the House supporting it. Attorney-General Chris Bishop said it gives effect to an agreement following the Stafford v Attorney-General litigation by transferring legal title from the Crown to the Te Here-ā-Nuku Trust. The bill also provides for some land to continue to be used for conservation, reserve, education and other public purposes. MPs noted that arrangements would allow continued Department of Conservation operations and public access, including through a 25-year licence for the Abel Tasman National Park. The bill is set down for committee stage at a later sitting.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rachel Boyack (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: In plain language, this bill helps give practical effect to what the court found and to what the parties have agreed.

keyExchanges.speaker: David Wilson (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: This is a moment that transcends the party lines in the House today, and when historical errors are laid bare by our highest courts, we have the maturity as a nation to correct them.

topicSummaries.topic: Teacher-Training Placements to Expand to 660 in 2027
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The expansion aims to increase the supply of classroom-ready teachers and support schools facing recruitment and retention challenges.
topicSummaries.content: Education Minister Erica Stanford said the School Onsite Training Programme would grow from 147 placements in 2024 to 660 in 2027, reaching 704 places annually from 2028. Student teachers in the programme receive a tax-free stipend of $20,660, and the Government is also expanding the Teacher Bonding Scheme to 235 places. Stanford said school-based training could better prepare trainees for classrooms and allow placements to be directed to areas of need, including rural and isolated schools.

topicSummaries.topic: Government Seeks More Advice on AI Data Centres and Electricity Prices
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The growth of energy-intensive data centres could affect electricity costs, making the Government’s assessment relevant to households and businesses.
topicSummaries.content: Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick questioned whether the Government had assessed the potential effects of AI data centres on electricity prices and the energy grid. Luxon said preliminary advice from the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment indicated that the centres were not expected to put upward pressure on prices, but the Government was seeking further advice and considering regulatory settings. He said about three data centres were expected to come online in the next year; no cost-benefit analysis or final regulatory approach was announced in the exchange. Swarbrick was ordered to leave the chamber after challenging the Speaker during the questioning.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chlöe Swarbrick (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Will the Datagrid AI centre raise electricity prices; if not, why not?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The advice we’ve had is that it won’t put an upward pressure on electricity prices, but that’s why we’re taking further advice from MBIE and, also, the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet

conclusion: The Government advanced major legislation on planning, climate liability and criminal law, while opposition parties challenged whether its pursuit of growth and certainty adequately protects environmental limits, Māori participation and citizens’ legal rights.
